title: How To Recover From A No Good, Unruly, Disorderly Teaching Day rderly-teaching-day/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin offers a six-step morning routine for resetting a classroom after a rough, unruly day, provided it was a minor setback rather than a total loss of control. The steps are: begin outside the classroom door to establish focus before entry, preview the day's positive activities rather than rehashing yesterday's problems, briefly restate classroom rules, review the first morning routine in detail, watch that routine closely without distraction, and repeat the routine if it isn't performed well. Linsin contrasts this constructive approach with the common mistake of turning grim or threatening after a bad day, arguing that such power plays damage rapport and fail to address the underlying cause. The steps are framed as addressing the root problem directly and restoring consistency rather than simply hoping tomorrow will be better.
points: A bad day can be recovered from with a deliberate morning reset, provided it was a minor setback rather than a total loss of classroom control.
Step 1: meet students outside the door to establish a focused mindset before they enter, rather than starting cold.
Step 2: preview the day's positive plans instead of rehashing yesterday's problems, to re-engage students' desire to behave.
Steps 3-5: briefly restate the rules, review the first morning routine in detail, and watch its execution closely without distraction.
Step 6: if the routine isn't performed well, calmly send students back to redo it rather than reacting emotionally—this restores consistency and standards.
quotes: The good news is that as long as it was a minor setback, and not a total loss of control, it isn’t difficult to do.
When recovering from a bad day, lining up outside will also send the message that the expectation bar has been picked up off the floor and placed back on the top rung where it belongs.
Rehashing yesterday’s woes is counterproductive. It merely drags the bad energy with you into the morning.
The first routine of the day is critical in restoring your classroom to its well-behaved state. A smooth and efficient performance will put to rest any concerns from the day before.
The biggest mistake teachers make after a bad day is to turn grim and standoffish, to use a show of disappointment and the threat of turning ‘mean’ as a hedge against a repeat performance.
The steps above, however, address the cause of the problems from the day before. They refresh and restore your classroom back to well-being.
